claim: Grid cells of the medial entorhinal cortex (MEC) fire at several locations organized as a grid of equilateral triangles.
source: Grid cells of the medial entorhinal cortex (MEC) fire at several locations organized as a grid of equilateral triangles (Hafting et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hafting et al., 2005

claim: The repetitive nature of the firing fields suggests that grid cells are an important metric element of a neuronal system involved in spatial navigation.
source: The repetitive nature of the firing fields suggests that grid cells are an important metric element of a neuronal system involved in spatial navigation (Hafting et al., 2005; McNaughton et al., 2006; Burgess et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies

claim: Grid cells appear to rely on self-motion cues to keep track of the animal's position during locomotion.
source: To keep track of the animal's position during locomotion, grid cells appear to rely on self-motion cues (Hafting et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hafting et al., 2005

claim: Computational models suggest that grid cells integrate heading direction and traveled distance.
source: Indeed, computational models suggest that grid cells integrate heading direction and traveled distance (Fuhs, 2006; McNaughton et al., 2006; Burgess et al., 2007; Burak and Fiete, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to computational modeling studies

claim: The directional component of grid cell activity likely depends on inputs from head-direction cells found in several subcortical and cortical areas, including the MEC.
source: The directional component likely depends on inputs from head-direction cells found in several subcortical and cortical areas, including the MEC (Taube et al., 1990; Valerio and Taube, 2012; Winter et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies on head-direction cells

claim: Traveled distance could be estimated from the firing rate of speed cells located in the MEC.
source: Traveled distance, on the other hand, could be estimated from the firing rate of speed cells located in the MEC (Kropff et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kropff et al., 2015

claim: The increase of the firing rate of speed cells as a function of running velocity is preserved across different environments.
source: As expected from an internal speedometer, the increase of the firing rate of speed cells as a function of running velocity is preserved across different environments (Kropff et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kropff et al., 2015

claim: Without corrections based on external inputs, intrinsic noise in neuronal networks causes an accumulation of error in the internal estimation of position.
source: Without corrections based on external inputs, intrinsic noise in neuronal networks causes an accumulation of error in the internal estimation of position (Burgess et al., 2007; Burak and Fiete, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to computational studies

claim: External landmarks, including the borders of the enclosure, prevent the position estimate from rapidly deviating from the actual location of the animal.
source: External landmarks, including the borders of the enclosure, serve this purpose (Knierim et al., 1995; Skaggs et al., 1995; Evans et al., 2015; Hardcastle et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies

claim: Rotation of a single polarizing visual landmark causes an equivalent reorientation of the grid pattern.
source: The influence of landmarks on grid cell activity is illustrated by cue control experiments in which the rotation of a single polarizing visual landmark causes an equivalent reorientation of the grid pattern (Hafting et al., 2005)
evidence: Supported by citation to Hafting et al., 2005

claim: Grid cells show reduced spatial selectivity in darkness.
source: and by the reduced spatial selectivity of grid cells in darkness (Hafting et al., 2005; Allen et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies

claim: Compression of a familiar rectangular environment along one axis can lead to a contraction of the grid pattern in the same axis.
source: Moreover, compression of a familiar rectangular environment along one axis can lead to a contraction of the grid pattern in the same axis (Barry et al., 2007; Stensola et al., 2012)
evidence: Supported by citations to Barry et al., 2007 and Stensola et al., 2012

claim: Grid orientation aligns to the environment borders with a small but constant offset.
source: and grid orientation aligns to the environment borders with a small but constant offset (Krupic et al., 2015; Stensola et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Krupic et al., 2015 and Stensola et al., 2015

claim: The color and odor of an enclosure can affect the positioning of the grid fields but not the grid orientation or the firing rate of the neurons.
source: Finally, there is also evidence that the color and odor of an enclosure can affect the positioning of the grid fields but not the grid orientation or the firing rate of the neurons (Marozzi et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Marozzi et al., 2015

claim: Most recording sites were in the MEC (75.51%, 37 out of 49) or at the transition between the MEC and the parasubiculum (12.24%, 6 out of 49).
source: Histological examination showed that most recording sites were in the MEC (75.51%, 37 out of 49) or at the transition between the MEC and the parasubiculum (12.24%, 6 out of 49) (Figure 1C, Figure 1—source data 1, Figure 1—source data 2).
evidence: Supported by histological data and figure reference

claim: 86.49% of tetrode tracks in the MEC had reached layer II by the last recording session.
source: Of the tetrode tracks in the MEC, 86.49% had reached layer II by the last recording session.
evidence: Supported by experimental data

claim: A total of 880 neurons were recorded in 8 mice (89 recording sessions).
source: A total of 880 neurons were recorded in 8 mice (89 recording sessions).
evidence: Supported by experimental data

claim: The firing fields of grid cells, border cells and irregular spatially selective neurons rotated around the center of the arena to follow the position of the light.
source: We found that the firing fields of grid cells, border cells and irregular spatially selective neurons rotated around the center of the arena to follow the position of the light (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in figures

claim: Peak correlations between l1 and l2 maps were obtained near 90° and 180° for recording sessions in which the angle between l1 and l2 was 90° and 180°, respectively.
source: Peak correlations were obtained near 90° and 180° for recording sessions in which the angle between l1 and l2 was 90° and 180°, respectively.
evidence: Supported by experimental data analysis

claim: During light trials, the light panels acted as dominant polarization cues.
source: Thus, during light trials, the light panels acted as dominant polarization cues.

claim: The periodic firing of grid cells was not visible in most rate maps of dark trials.

claim: Grid scores and information scores were much lower during d1 trials compared to l1 trials.
source: Grid scores and information scores were much lower during d1 trials compared to l1 trials (Figure 2B; paired Wilcoxon signed rank test, l1 vs d1, n = 139 grid cells, grid score: v = 9223, p<10−16, information score: v = 9722, p<10−16).

evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: Visual landmarks were required to stabilize the grid firing pattern.
source: Thus, visual landmarks were required to stabilize the grid firing pattern.

claim: The grid pattern observed during light trials was present during the first few seconds in darkness.
source: The grid pattern observed during light trials was present during the first few seconds in darkness.
evidence: Supported by experimental data analysis

claim: During d1 trials, map similarity was initially high and decreased during the first 30 s.
source: During d1 trials, map similarity was initially high and decreased during the first 30 s (paired Wilcoxon signed rank test, n = 132, b1-b2: p<10−16, b2-b3: p=0.00053).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: The stable periodic pattern was only present during the first 30 s in darkness.
source: This indicates that the stable periodic pattern was only present during the first 30 s in darkness.

claim: When the l1 LED panel was turned back on, map similarity during the first 10 s was lower than during the subsequent l1 block.
source: Interestingly, when the l1 LED panel was turned back on, map similarity during the first 10 s was lower than during the subsequent l1 block (Figure 2D, p<10−15).

claim: The reinstatement of the grid pattern by visual stimuli occurred over the course of several seconds.
source: Thus, the reinstatement of the grid pattern by visual stimuli occurred over the course of several seconds.

claim: Pairs of grid cells with a similar spacing exhibit very stable firing associations; cells that fire together in one environment also fire together in a different environment.
source: Pairs of grid cells with a similar spacing exhibit very stable firing associations; cells that fire together in one environment also fire together in a different environment (Fyhn et al., 2007; Yoon et al., 2013; Allen et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies

claim: Firing rate associations for pairs of grid cells were stable from l1 to l2 trials.
source: As expected, firing rate associations for pairs of grid cells were stable from l1 to l2 trials (Figure 2E, Pearson correlation of firing rate associations in l1 and l2 trials, n = 186 grid cell pairs, r = 0.968, p<10−16).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: Despite instability in the spatial firing patterns of grid cells during dark trials, the firing rate associations of grid cells were to a large extent preserved during d1 trials.
source: Despite instability in the spatial firing patterns of grid cells during dark trials, the firing rate associations of grid cells were to a large extent preserved during d1 trials (Figure 2E, r = 0.926, p<10−16).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: The median firing rate of grid cells was slightly lower during dark trials than during light trials.
source: The median firing rate of grid cells was slightly lower during dark trials than during light trials (Figure 2F; paired Wilcoxon signed rank test v = 6048, p=0.0129).

claim: Grid scores calculated from the spike-triggered maps were lower during d1 than l1 trials.
source: Accordingly, grid scores calculated from the spike-triggered maps were lower during d1 than l1 trials (n = 139 grid cells, median l1: 0.054, median d1: −0.062, v = 12246, p=0.00011).

claim: The impairment in grid periodicity in darkness cannot be fully explained by a slow translational drift.
source: Thus, the impairment in grid periodicity in darkness cannot be fully explained by a slow translational drift.

claim: Distance scores were smaller during dark trials than during light trials.
source: Distance scores were smaller during dark trials than during light trials (Figure 3C; paired Wilcoxon signed rank test, n = 50 grid cells, v = 1181, p<10−7)

claim: Out of 880 MEC neurons, 304 (34.55%) had a speed score above chance levels.
source: Out of 880 MEC neurons, 304 (34.55%) had a speed score above chance levels (Figure 4B).
